articles.title: Russia and Ukraine Confirm Humanitarian Ceasefire Has Taken Effect in Oleshky - Antiwar.com
articles.summary: Russia and Ukraine Confirm Humanitarian Ceasefire Has Taken Effect in Oleshky  Antiwar.com
articles.full_text:
Both Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday confirmed that a humanitarian ceasefire had taken effect around Oleshky, a frontline town in Ukraine’s Kherson region that’s been under Russian control since the first days of the 2022 invasion.
The purpose of the truce is to get humanitarian aid to the 2,000 remaining residents of the town and allow those who want to leave to evacuate. Civilians in the town have faced severe food shortages, with some telling Reuters they’ve been surviving on just a cup of rice or buckwheat a day.
First Lady Melania Trump, who was involved in the negotiations for the truce, said in a post on X that the “geographic area has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson Region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys.”
Pope Leo XIV also helped mediate between the two sides, calling Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky shortly after his recent lung surgery to urge them to agree to a truce that would allow humanitarian aid into the area. The White House released a statement on October 23 announcing the ceasefire, credited Melania Trump with the mediation, and didn’t mention Pope Leo’s role.
The initial announcement said the truce would take effect on October 29, but Melania said on X that the “timing was accelerated two days ahead of schedule to protect the safety of civilians and to facilitate the delivery of critical humanitarian aid.”
The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement on Tuesday that as “part of preparations for a humanitarian operation near the town of Alyoshki (Oleshky) in the Kherson Region, the Russian Armed Forces ceased fire in the Kherson direction at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27.”
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said that starting at 3:00 am local time, it was “implementing a ceasefire in a designated area to conduct a humanitarian operation in the temporarily occupied town of Oleshky in the Kherson region.”

articles.title: Russian officials to inspect Georgia’s fruit safety amid suspension of imports of some Georgian drinks - OC Media
articles.summary: Russian officials to inspect Georgia’s fruit safety amid suspension of imports of some Georgian drinks  OC Media
articles.full_text:
Russia’s agricultural watchdog, Rosselkhoznadzor, will visit Georgia from 2 November to inspect the country’s phytosanitary certification system for fruit exported to Russia, the agency announced on Monday.
The visit comes after Russia temporarily suspended imports and sales of certain alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages from Georgian producers earlier this month, citing quality control reasons. Moscow has denied that the restrictions were politically motivated.
Russia has imposed wide-reaching import restrictions on Armenian goods in recent years. Moscow has cited quality and safety concerns in those cases as well, while critics have suggested the measures were politically motivated amid deteriorating relations between Russia and Armenia.
The announcement follows a three-day regional workshop organised by the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) in Tbilisi from 20–22 October, which brought together regional and international experts to discuss strengthening veterinary product regulatory systems. Representatives of Russia’s Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (Rosselkhoznadzor) also participated in the workshop.
Georgia and Russia have had no diplomatic relations since the 2008 August war but maintain trade and economic relations.
The Russian delegation will examine Georgia’s phytosanitary certification system for pome and stone fruits exported to Russia. It will also audit a laboratory that tests plant-based products for pesticide and agrochemical residues before they enter the Russian market. The last time Russia did this kind of inspection was in 2014.
Rosselkhoznadzor said the visit, arranged at the invitation of Georgia’s National Food Agency, aims to establish common approaches to controlling goods subject to quarantine requirements. The two sides are also expected to hold video talks on the programme for the visit.
‘The visit aims to establish common approaches to controlling goods subject to quarantine requirements’, Rosselkhoznadzor added.
The agency reported that Russia had imported 70,500 tonnes of fruit and vegetable products from Georgia as of 24 October 2026.
Its data showed increases in imports of nectarines, apples, blueberries, plums, mandarins, fresh figs, and watermelons compared with the same period a year earlier.
On 22 October, Rosselkhoznadzor stated two Georgian dairy-processing plants would gain access to the Russian market from November. The agency said it had initiated a request to the relevant Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) authorities to approve the plants’ inclusion in the register of enterprises from third countries.
Russia also expressed readiness to inspect six Georgian fish and seafood producers interested in exporting to Russia. Their products would be eligible to enter the Russian market if the inspections found no violations, the agency said.
On 10 October, it emerged that Russia had temporarily suspended the import and sale of some alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks from several Georgian producers.
The affected products included wine from Teliani Valley, Tbilvino, and Wine Man; wine and brandy from Askaneli Brothers; beer from the Georgian Beer Company; Coca-Cola produced in Georgia; and Nabeglavi mineral water, produced by Healthy Water.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova described the restrictions as routine quality-control measures and denied that they were politically motivated.
Georgia’s National Food Agency had not provided a response to OC Media’s questions about the planned Rosselkhoznadzor visit at the time of writing.

articles.title: Israel Inks Record Voting: The verdict & trajectory of Iran war, US ties, West Asia security & relations with India - Organiser
articles.summary: Israel Inks Record Voting: The verdict & trajectory of Iran war, US ties, West Asia security & relations with India  Organiser
articles.full_text:
The high-stake October 27 elections of Israel and its high voltage results are not just anticipated in the domestic political landscape of Tel Aviv, but is awaited across West Asia, US and the larger world including India. The electoral outcomes and political trajectory of Tel Aviv could reshape the future of the country and its influence or response to the conflict in Gaza and war with Iran. The election results are also decoded to be detrimental for the ties with Washington DC.
With neither the right-wing bloc nor the opposition assured of the 61 seats needed for a Knesset(parliamentary) majority, coalition arithmetic will be decisive and has ignited utmost curiosity and calculations across the global political apparatus. Howevr, the country has witnessed a record voter turn out on October 27, breaching all the previous election benchmarks.
For India, the outcome matters beyond bilateral ties, with implications for defence cooperation, energy security, relations with the Gulf and the future of the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC).
Decoding the domestic political dynamics; Who will gain the majority?
Israelis are voting in the country’s first general election since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack and the ensuing conflict in Gaza. The elections are also maiden, since the direct confrontation broke out with Iran on February 28, 2026. Political experts, thus, interpret the elections as a critical referendum on Israel’s security and geopolitical stakes in the West Asian latitude.
Early figures pointed to strong participation. Turnout reportedly reached 16.7 per cent by 10AM, with around 1.2 million votes cast, and rose to 31.5 per cent by noon, compared with 28.4 per cent at the same stage of the 2022 election. These figures indicate voter engagement, but do not hint about which political party holds the advantage.
Approximately 7.3 million eligible voters are choosing 120 members of the Knesset, Israel’s Parliament. Under the proportional representation system, parties must cross a 3.25 per cent electoral threshold to win seats. A government requires the support of atleast 61 lawmakers.
Polling stations were scheduled to close at 10PM local time, with exit polls expected afterwards. These projections can indicate the likely balance of power, but the official result and subsequent coalition negotiations will determine who governs.
Netanyahu’s Likud party is competing against an opposition led by former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar Party, alongside figures including former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman.
As per the reports, neither major political coalition was assured of the 61 seats required to form a government. Smaller parties, including Arab-led groups, could therefore become pivotal in coalition negotiations. Netanyahu could seek to retain power through his established right-wing and ultra-Orthodox partners. The opposition, meanwhile, faces the challenge of reconciling differing political priorities to assemble a viable majority.
A hung parliament could lead to prolonged negotiations, a caretaker government or another election. The result will therefore depend not only on which bloc wins more seats, but on which leader can build a stable coalition.
What are the security stakes for Israel, Gaza, Iran & West Asia?
Israel’s next government will inherit a volatile regional security environment earmarked by the Gaza war, confrontation with Iran, tensions with Hamas and Hezbollah in Lebanon and instability in Syria.
Netanyahu has repeatedly reiterated that Israel must retain the capacity to eliminate threats. Meanwhile, opposition leader Eisenkot has also advocated a tough security posture, while placing greater emphasis on coordination with Washington and combining military pressure with diplomatic and inspection mechanisms.
As Israeli leaders advocate utmost priority to the security of the country and jewish/Israeli identity, the election results or the change of government would not automatically produce a major or sudden shift in Tel Aviv’s security doctrine.
For example, Netanyahu has argued that Hamas must be disarmed and prevented from governing Gaza to insulate Israel from repeated threats. Eisenkot has also opposed continued Hamas rule and proposed ending it through a US-led framework or if necessary, military action. Thus, the security priorities and strategy of Israel is said to remain consistent, irrespective of the election results.
A new government might alter Israel’s diplomatic approach, but the fundamental question and doctrines remain intact. Israeli policies on Palestinian statehood appears unlikely to change. Support for a two-state settlement remains limited among several mainstream Jewish-majority parties.
On the other hand, the confrontation with Iran is also likely to remain as a defining security issue for Tel Aviv, regardless of the election outcome. Netanyahu has consistently treated Iran’s nuclear programme and regional influence as major threats, favouring military pressure and the option of direct action. Eisenkot has also argued that Iran must not acquire nuclear weapons, while advocating coordination with Washington, intrusive inspections and the retention of military options.
Beyond the electoral decision and the popular verdict, Israel’s security policies and geopolitical strategy is set to be consistent. Despite, political differences and who assumes the helm of Israeli Knesset, Tel Aviv’s approach to Iran, Gaza, the Palestinian and the larger West Asian landscape, is anticipated to be solid and deteremined.
US-Israel Relations: Continuity or a change in the tone?
How will the Israel election reuslts impact its ties with Washington DC and the Trump administration is yet another striking question in the geopolitical landscape. However, as per the analysts, US role in Israel’s security remains fundamental, spanning military assistance, intelligence cooperation and regional diplomacy. The election could change the political dynamics of that relationship, but is unlikely to erase its strategic foundations.
Netanyahu has cultivated a close relationship with Trump and presented US backing as an advantage in confronting Iran. A Netanyahu victory would preserve and continue this established channel. An Eisenkot-led government could seek closer coordination with a wider group of Western partners and place greater emphasis on joint planning with Washington. Yet a change in leadership would not necessarily mean a softer position on Iran or an outright departure from existing security priorities.
India-Israel strategic ties: The future course amid elections
For India, the election matters because Israel is a major defence and technology partner, while the larger West Asia remains central to India’s energy supplies, trade and diaspora interests. During Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Israel in February 2026, the two countries elevated their relationship to a “Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity”. Cooperation spans defence, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum technologies, agriculture, water management and space.
These institutional links provide a foundation for continuity, regardless of who forms Israel’s next government. However, regional instability and Israel’s own military requirements could affect the pace of defence deliveries, joint projects and investment.
In terms of defence ties, Israel has supplied India with defence systems for surveillance, precision operations and air defence. The relationship has increasingly moved beyond procurement towards technology transfer, joint research and co-development, supporting India’s Aatmanirbhar Bharat agenda.
Both countries have incentives to sustain cooperation. India gains access to specialised technologies, while Israel benefits from a major strategic partner and a market for defence and advanced technology. A new Israeli government could adjust individual priorities, but a major rupture appears unlikely. The immediate concern for New Delhi is whether ongoing projects, supplies and technology partnerships remain on schedule amid regional security pressures.
India and Israel have also pursued closer economic ties through trade negotiations, investment and collaboration in advanced manufacturing and digital services. Cooperation in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, agriculture, water management and labour mobility offers scope to broaden the partnership beyond defence. Political stability will matter for the implementation of existing agreements and the confidence of investors. A prolonged coalition deadlock could delay decisions, even if it does not fundamentally alter the bilateral ties.
India’s West Asia strategy
India-Israel relations cannot be viewed in isolation. New Delhi’s West Asia strategy spans a wide spectrum including the Iran and the Gulf countries, each serving a distinctive strategic purpose, to secure national interests. The Gulf Cooperation Council is a major economic partner and a critical source of energy. Approximately 10 million Indian nationals live across the Gulf, making regional stability important for their safety, employment and remittances. Meanwhile, India-GCC trade was reported at around US$178.63 billion in FY2025-26.
India’s engagement with Iran also remains significant. Chabahar port is intended to strengthen access to Afghanistan and Central Asia while providing an alternative to routes through Pakistan. Sanctions and regional tensions, however, complicate the project’s prospects. A wider Israel-Iran confrontation could raise energy prices, disrupt shipping and expose Indian nationals to greater risks. Any threat to the Strait of Hormuz would have direct consequences for India’s economic, civilian and energy security.

articles.title: Month after Russia’s ban on Georgian drinks, Russian experts to inspect laboratories in Georgia: what are risks? - JAMnews
articles.summary: Month after Russia’s ban on Georgian drinks, Russian experts to inspect laboratories in Georgia: what are risks?  JAMnews
articles.full_text:
Russia’s Rosselkhoznadzor to inspect Georgian laboratories
From 2 November 2026, specialists from Russia’s agricultural watchdog, Rosselkhoznadzor, will visit Georgia to inspect Georgian laboratories, the agency said in a statement.
The Russian specialists will examine Georgia’s phytosanitary certification system for fruit and other plant products intended for export to Russia. They will also inspect a laboratory that tests such products for pesticide and agrochemical residues.
- Russia bans imports of several drinks from Georgia
- Russia destroyed 40,000 Armenian roses shipped via Belarus
Phytosanitary certification confirms that plant-based products meet the requirements of the importing country. Laboratory tests for pesticide and agrochemical residues, meanwhile, detect the presence of these chemicals in products.
According to Rosselkhoznadzor, the visit follows an invitation from Georgia’s National Food Agency. The agency said the aim was to develop a common approach to monitoring products subject to quarantine controls.
The Russian agency did not specify which laboratory its specialists would visit. It also remains unclear whether the inspection will lead to any changes in the conditions for exporting Georgian products to Russia.
The Georgian side has yet to provide official information. Georgia’s National Food Agency promised JAMnews it would clarify the details, but subsequently stopped answering calls.
Background: the context for the planned visit by Russian specialists to Georgia
The planned inspection of laboratories in Georgia coincides with Russia’s ban on imports of several Georgian-made drinks.
The restrictions cover both alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages. They affect seven major Georgian companies, including producers of Coca-Cola and Nabeglavi water in Georgia. The companies affected by the ban account for around 75–80% of Georgia’s wine exports to Russia. Russia’s embargo on Georgian drinks came into force on 10 October.
Later, from 20 to 22 October, Rosselkhoznadzor specialists visited Tbilisi to attend a regional seminar organised by the World Organisation for Animal Health. During the visit, they also discussed bilateral co-operation with representatives of Georgia’s National Food Agency.
Following these meetings, Rosselkhoznadzor announced on 22 October that it would allow two Georgian dairy processors to access the Russian market from November. The agency also said it was ready to inspect six Georgian fish and seafood producers interested in exporting their products to Russia.
The statement also noted a 26% increase in Russian exports of live pigs to Georgia, while onion supplies had tripled. Meanwhile, Georgia’s exports to Russia of products such as blueberries, apples, plums and mandarins continue to grow.
According to Rosselkhoznadzor, Russia had imported 70,500 tonnes of fruit and vegetables from Georgia by 24 October 2026.
Imports increased across several product categories:
- Nectarines — 17,900 tonnes, up 7.8%;
- Apples — 15,300 tonnes, up 17.5%;
- Blueberries — 9,500 tonnes, up 46.7%;
- Plums — 6,700 tonnes, up 74.2%;
- Mandarins — around 3,400 tonnes, up 59%;
- Figs — more than 1,900 tonnes, up 21.2%;
- Watermelons — 1,400 tonnes, up 59.5%.
What are the risks? — expert assessments
Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the Unity – National Movement party, sees the invitation to Russian specialists as a sign that relations with Moscow are entering a new phase.
In her view, the decision raises questions about the reliability of Georgia’s own inspection systems. It also gives Russia additional leverage to exert economic pressure on the country.
“How can you invite a Russian expert to Georgia and give them the authority to inspect our products? What does this tell us? That they do not trust the food safety standards we have established ourselves. It also makes Georgia’s economy even more dependent on Russia. We know that Russia turns economic leverage into a tool of blackmail — as it demonstrated just a few weeks ago when it imposed an embargo on goods produced in Georgia.”
Teona Akubardia, a security expert, also points to risks to national security. She says Russia could selectively restrict access to its market for Georgian products and use that leverage for political purposes.
“There is a risk that Russia will be able to grant or deny access to its market at its own discretion. The state will have no means of protecting itself. With the process of integration with the West frozen, Russia will use this leverage even more actively for political purposes, seeking to bring Georgia fully under its control. This poses a threat to national security. Moreover, the Georgian Dream party is not only failing to neutralise this threat but is creating additional risks under the current circumstances.”

articles.title: Tajikistan discusses oil and gas cooperation with Kuwait Petroleum Corporation - Азия-Плюс
articles.summary: Tajikistan discusses oil and gas cooperation with Kuwait Petroleum Corporation  Азия-Плюс
articles.full_text:
Tajikistan and Kuwait have discussed expanding cooperation in the oil and gas sector, as the Central Asian country seeks to diversify its fuel supplies. The talks took place on October 25 in Kuwait between Tajikistan’s Ambassador Khusrav Noziri and Kuwait’s Minister of Oil and Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC) Chairman Tariq Suleiman Al-Rumi.
According to Tajikistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the sides reviewed bilateral relations and prospects for cooperation in the oil and gas industry. Kuwait Times, citing the state news agency KUNA, reported that they also discussed broader economic ties, energy cooperation and the exchange of expertise.
No specific projects, investment commitments, fuel supply arrangements or contracts were announced.
KPC is Kuwait’s state-owned oil company, with operations spanning oil exploration and production, refining, petrochemicals, transportation and marketing.
Tajikistan seeks to diversify fuel imports
According to the Agency for Statistics under the President of Tajikistan, no significant trade between Tajikistan and Kuwait was recorded in the first nine months of 2026.
Meanwhile, Tajikistan imported 916,400 tons of petroleum products worth $858.4 million during the same period. Import volumes increased by 3.8% year on year, while their value rose by 24.2%. Petroleum products accounted for 10.1% of the country’s total imports.
Russia remains Tajikistan’s main fuel supplier, but the country has also increased purchases from Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. Since late August, it has additionally received oil and petroleum products from Iran, according to previous Asia-Plus reporting.
Government forecasts suggest petroleum product imports could reach 1.55 million tons in 2027, increasing the importance of finding additional suppliers.
Broader economic ties
The talks with Kuwait’s oil sector come amid efforts to expand economic relations between the two countries. In late September, Tajikistan proposed holding a joint business forum and an exhibition of Tajik products in Kuwait and expressed interest in attracting Kuwaiti investment.
Kuwait already supports development projects in Tajikistan through the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development. In June 2026, the fund provided a concessional loan of approximately $19.4 million for school infrastructure development.

articles.title: Uzbekistan Seeks Stronger Trade And Investment Ties With Turkic States - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: Uzbekistan Seeks Stronger Trade And Investment Ties With Turkic States  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan is seeking to expand industrial cooperation, investment and trade with members of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS), as regional economic relations move beyond conventional trade towards joint manufacturing, transport connectivity and digital development.
The initiative comes ahead of the organisation's summit in Ankara on 30 October, where leaders are expected to discuss economic cooperation, investment and regional integration.
President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has proposed creating a “Space of New Economic Opportunities” to encourage companies across participating countries to establish joint production chains, manufacture higher-value goods and expand exports to international markets.
Uzbekistan's Trade With Turkic Partners Reaches $10.82 Billion
According to figures published by Uzbekistan's diplomatic missions, the country's trade with other OTS members, Turkmenistan and Hungary increased from $4.13 billion in 2017 to $10.82 billion in 2025.
Trade expanded by 19.8% year on year during the first seven months of 2026.
Exports to these markets totalled $2.29 billion between January and July, compared with imports of $4.46 billion, indicating opportunities for Uzbekistan to strengthen its export-oriented industries.
As of early August, Uzbekistan had 4,871 enterprises operating with capital participation from partner countries.
Joint Investment Projects Valued At $17.24 Billion
Investment cooperation is also expanding.
In 2025, Uzbekistan attracted $4.29 billion in investment from Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Türkiye, Turkmenistan and Hungary.
During 2026, work has been progressing on 280 projects with a combined value of $17.24 billion, of which $3.84 billion had been invested between January and August.
One example is an Azerbaijani-backed gypsum manufacturing project in Uzbekistan's Kashkadarya region, where the first stage has been completed and work on gypsum board production has begun.
The Turkic Investment Fund, which became operational in 2026, is expected to support investment projects, industrial cooperation and business financing.
At a meeting in February, OTS economy and trade officials signed a trade-related memorandum aimed at strengthening economic ties.
Transport And Digital Cooperation Drive Future Growth
Uzbekistan is also seeking stronger transport connections through the Middle Corridor, the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway and a proposed Trans-Afghan route.
The E-Permit electronic transport authorisation system, initially developed through Uzbekistan-Türkiye cooperation, now operates among all OTS member states.
On the technology front, Mirziyoyev proposed a Digital Turkic Corridor linking regional data centres through high-speed communications networks.
He also invited partner countries to join an investment fund being established with Kazakhstan to support start-ups and innovative technologies.
Uzbekistan's broader objective is to translate growing trade and investment into greater manufacturing capacity, stronger export competitiveness and improved access to international markets.
The success of these initiatives will depend on completed projects, operational businesses and the economic value created through regional cooperation.

articles.title: Russia, Morocco Bilateral Relations & Trade As Western Sahara Debate Resurfaces: October 2026 Update - russia's pivot to asia
articles.summary: Russia, Morocco Bilateral Relations & Trade As Western Sahara Debate Resurfaces: October 2026 Update  russia's pivot to asia
articles.full_text:
The Russian Foreign Minister, Sergey Lavrov, had a telephone conversation with Nasser Bourita, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Morocco, following a request from the Moroccan side.
The conversation, which took place on October 23, focused on priority objectives for further steady development of Russian-Moroccan relations and preparations for the Third Russia-Africa Summit, as well as key regional issues in the context of maintaining bilateral foreign policy coordination, including at the United Nations.
A major part of the talks was to discuss bilateral cooperation and coordination at the United Nations amid negotiations over a new Security Council resolution on the Moroccan Sahara. The text is expected to advance a final settlement based on Morocco’s expanded autonomy plan under its sovereignty. Russia abstained on the previous resolution without using their veto.
The new resolution is to be put to the vote on October 29. If successful, it would change the format of the United Nations presence in the Western Sahara, where it is currently titled the ‘UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara’ (MINURSO), which was created in 1991 as part of a ceasefire between Moroccan forces and the Polisario Front. The latter is a Sahrawi nationalist and Arab socialist organization, whose main goal is the independence of Western Sahara from Moroccan occupation. The United Nations has previously considered the Polisario Front to be the legitimate representative of the Sahrawi people and maintains that the Sahrawis have a right to self-determination. The Polisario Front is outlawed in the parts of Western Sahara. The new resolution would imply that Morocco has sovereignty over the region.
Western Sahara covers an area of 272,000 square kilometres and has a population of about 600,000—one of the least densely populated regions in Africa. It possesses a remarkably rich reserve of natural resources that stand at the center of its decades-long geopolitical conflict. About 80% of the region is primarily controlled and exploited by Morocco, while the management of these resources remains highly contested globally. International bodies, such as the European Court of Justice, routinely rule that extracting these resources without the explicit consent of the indigenous Saharawi people violates international laws.
The Western Sahara possesses vast, uninterrupted desert plains and strong coastal wind currents, offering massive potential for utility-scale solar and wind energy farms. Currently, Morocco utilizes these newly built green energy grids primarily to power its high-intensity phosphate mining operations. Western Sahara possesses some of the world’s largest phosphate deposits, used globally as a fertilizer, as well as access to some of West Africa’s primary fishing grounds.
Aside from the Western Sahara issue, the two ministers discussed strengthening Moroccan-Russian relations, preparations for the third Russia-Africa Summit, scheduled for October 28–29 in Moscow, and other regional developments.
Russia-Morocco Bilateral Trade
Trade between Russia and Morocco is fairly static and remains at the US$2 billion level, according to Igor Belyaev, the Russian Ambassador, who mentioned the figure in August. He added that Russia supplies Morocco with agricultural raw materials and industrial and chemical products, including urea, which is widely used in the kingdom’s agricultural sector. Russian companies also export insulin, anticancer drugs, vaccines and pesticides, while Morocco exports fruit, vegetables, and seafood to Russia.
Belyaev noted that work was under way to expand the range of goods supplied, including through halal certification. He added that the bilateral potential had not yet been fully realized and that co-operation needed to be intensified. He added that “political dialogue between Russia and Morocco is at a high level. At the same time, I believe that the potential of trade and economic cooperation has not yet been fully realised and does not correspond to the level of political relations.”
The ambassador identified supplies of liquefied natural gas (LNG) and green hydrogen as promising areas of partnership. He said that “in the natural gas sector, cooperation on liquefied natural gas supplies could become a promising area of interaction.” Projects being implemented in Morocco to create infrastructure for receiving and regasifying LNG are creating the conditions for new suppliers to enter the market and opening up potential opportunities for the development of Russian-Moroccan cooperation in the gas sector.”

articles.title: Russia, India Bilateral Trade Up 24.3% In 7M 2026 As Parliamentarians Meet in New Delhi - russia's pivot to asia
articles.summary: Russia, India Bilateral Trade Up 24.3% In 7M 2026 As Parliamentarians Meet in New Delhi  russia's pivot to asia
articles.full_text:
Trade between India and Russia has grown by more than 20% this year, Russian State Duma Chairman Vyacheslav Volodin said during talks in New Delhi on Sunday (October 25), where he called for the removal of trade barriers and the expansion of joint business ventures. Volodin met the speaker of the Lok Sabha (Indian Parliament) Om Birla, ahead of the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum, which New Delhi is hosting on October 26-27. The discussions covered closer cooperation on trade, industry and agriculture, along with the strengthening of parliamentary ties.
According to data from the Indian Ministry of Commerce, bilateral commerce reached US$47.7 billion in the first seven months of 2026, up 24.3% from the same period in 2025.
India imported US$44.9 billion of Russian goods during the seven-month period, including US$36 billion in crude oil. Indian exports to Russia totalled US$2.8 billion, with increasing purchases of chemicals, electrical goods, medical equipment, seafood, tea, and spices.
Volodin told Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla that bilateral ties are advancing across all sectors, stressing that parliamentarians must ensure agreements reached by the countries’ leaders are translated into law. He said that lawmakers should “provide legislative support for all decisions made at the level of heads of state.”
Birla highlighted opportunities to expand cooperation in nuclear energy and other industrial sectors, while calling for regular exchanges between the two parliaments.
The expansion in commerce comes as New Delhi and Moscow work toward reaching US$100 billion in annual bilateral trade by 2030. India is seeking to narrow its trade imbalance with Russia by increasing exports of pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, chemicals, food products, and auto components.
The countries have also strengthened local currency payment mechanisms to facilitate trade. ‘Ruble-rupee settlements now account for 96% of bilateral transactions,’ Ivan Nosov, head of Sberbank India, said last month.
The two countries are working to address standards-related issues and non-tariff barriers affecting Indian agricultural and marine exports. India is also negotiating a free trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), which includes Russia, to improve market access.
Indian Ambassador to Russia Vinay Kumar said earlier this month that expanding the range of traded products and easing market restrictions would be central to increasing bilateral commerce.

articles.title: C5+1 Statement Omits Afghanistan, Prioritizes Trans-Caspian Trade - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: C5+1 Statement Omits Afghanistan, Prioritizes Trans-Caspian Trade  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
The United States and the five Central Asian republics have issued a joint statement on economic and security cooperation that makes no mention of Afghanistan, once a central concern of U.S. regional policy. The document followed the October 19 C5+1 ministerial meeting in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
Afghanistan’s absence from the statement does not mean it has disappeared from negotiations or Washington’s strategic interests. Nevertheless, a comparison with earlier C5+1 documents reveals a shift in the published agenda. Where Washington once placed considerable importance on connecting Central Asia with South Asia through Afghanistan, the latest statement focuses on trade across the Caspian Sea and investment in the region’s minerals.
Afghanistan’s Changing Place in C5+1 Talks
In July 2021, just weeks before the Taliban retook Kabul, C5+1 participants at a conference in Tashkent explicitly supported closer trade and transport links between Central and South Asia through Afghanistan, as well as efforts to secure peace in the country. That month, the U.S., Uzbekistan, Afghanistan, and Pakistan also announced plans for a quadrilateral platform to support trade and transportation projects linking the two regions.
In July 2023, Afghanistan was the subject of a separate C5+1 special session in Astana. Officials called for an inclusive Afghan government that respected women’s rights and backed further development of transport and energy links through the country. A joint statement issued by C5+1 leaders that September described Afghanistan as an important factor in Central Asian security.
In the 2026 Samarkand statement, Afghanistan goes unmentioned even in the section on border security and terrorism. However, the October 2023 C5+1 connectivity statement had already highlighted the Trans-Caspian Trade Route, which connects Central Asia to Western markets, and also omitted Afghanistan.
For Central Asian countries, the Afghan route remains important in practical terms. Uzbekistan is pursuing plans for a railway through Afghanistan to Pakistan, which would give it access to Indian Ocean ports. Kazakhstan is already a major supplier of food to Afghanistan, exporting around $216 million worth of flour and $122 million of wheat in the first seven months of 2026. In September, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan also agreed with the United Arab Emirates to study a railway corridor through Afghanistan to Pakistan.
Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan all share borders with Afghanistan. Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan also face the prospect of reduced water supplies from the Amu Darya as Afghanistan builds its Qosh Tepa Canal. Afghanistan’s omission from a joint statement should therefore not be taken as a complete account of the policies of all five Central Asian states.
What Constrains Washington
One possible explanation lies in the U.S. approach to Afghanistan’s current authorities. Washington allows practical contacts with representatives of the Taliban but does not recognize the government it has formed. The movement remains designated as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist, although it is not included in the U.S. Department of State’s separate list of Foreign Terrorist Organizations.
The designation restricts dealings with the Taliban, although U.S. sanctions rules permit many commercial transactions involving Afghanistan’s governing institutions, including civilian infrastructure and transportation projects. Restrictions remain on direct financial transfers to the Taliban, subject to specified exceptions.
Washington would have to reconcile support for projects involving Afghan authorities with its policy of nonrecognition of the Taliban government and the remaining restrictions. These constraints did not, however, prevent C5+1 participants from backing transport and energy links through Afghanistan in 2023.
Pakistan is important to Central Asia’s access to Indian Ocean ports through Afghanistan. But relations between Kabul and Islamabad have deteriorated sharply. Fighting along their border in October 2025 led to the closure of major crossings, and trade disruptions continued into 2026.
An alternative route south runs through Iran and its ports. Here, the constraints arise from U.S.-Iranian relations and Washington’s sanctions policy.
Different Routes, Different Priorities
The shift in the published agenda cannot be explained solely by Washington’s relationship with Afghanistan. Central Asia has significance in its own right for U.S. economic policy, particularly as a potential source of critical minerals and a destination for American investment.
The Trans-Caspian route does not replace southern corridors. It connects different markets, and its viability depends on transit countries’ infrastructure and policies, including tariffs.
For Central Asian capitals, choosing between these routes is not necessary. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan can develop ties with Afghanistan while participating in Trans-Caspian projects and expanding cooperation with the U.S.
Moreover, the gradual normalization of contacts with Kabul as part of routine trade and transportation activities could reduce the need to discuss Afghanistan separately at every C5+1 meeting.
Afghanistan’s absence from the Samarkand statement therefore allows for at least two interpretations. Washington may have deliberately focused on initiatives that do not require political engagement with the Taliban. Alternatively, Central Asian countries may be increasingly handling Afghan-related issues on their own, reserving the C5+1 format for projects where U.S. participation is most valuable.
